x.A: AdministratorAccess is an identity-based policy, not a resource-based policy, so it can't be attached as one to a group.
x.B: SystemAdministrator is a job-function policy with limited scope, not full access to all AWS services and resources.
x.C: The AdministratorAccess identity-based policy attached to an IAM group gives full access to every member, so putting the five users in the group meets the requirement.
x.D: SystemAdministrator isn't full access, and resource-based policies aren't attached to IAM groups.

x.A: Lambda for the compute layers is serverless, so there's no infrastructure to manage, which is the least effort.
x.B: EC2 instances for compute means managing servers, which is more infrastructure management.
x.C: SNS doesn't guarantee exactly-once delivery and doesn't hold messages for consumers to process asynchronously.
x.D: SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and ordering, so they replace the third-party middleware as the messaging component.
x.E: EKS containers still need cluster and node management, which means more infrastructure to manage.

x.A: Transfer for SFTP is a managed, highly available SFTP service, EFS provides shared storage, and an Auto Scaling group with scheduled scaling runs the nightly batch on EC2, mounting the same file system. It needs little management.
x.B: A self-run SFTP server on one EC2 instance with EBS isn't highly available and needs management.
x.C: A self-run SFTP service on one instance with EFS storage is still a single instance to manage, so it isn't resilient or low effort.
x.D: Transfer for SFTP with S3 is managed, but the application would need to change to pull files from S3, which adds effort compared with using a shared file system.

x.A: AWS WAF can't be attached to a Network Load Balancer, because it works with ALBs, CloudFront, and API Gateway.
x.B: ALBs in each Region with WAF protect against web exploits, and Global Accelerator provides static IP addresses and routes users to the closest healthy Region, improving availability and performance.
x.C: WAF can't be deployed on NLBs, and CloudFront doesn't provide static IP addresses.
x.D: CloudFront with WAF protects the application, but CloudFront doesn't provide static IP addresses.

x.A: Switching to RDS Multi-AZ cluster doesn't fix too many connections and is a large migration.
x.B: RDS Proxy pools and shares connections, which fixes the too many connections errors, and it speeds up failover by maintaining connections and reducing failover time for Aurora.
x.C: DynamoDB with DAX is a different database model, so it needs a major rewrite.
x.D: Redshift is a data warehouse and doesn't fit a transactional MySQL database.

x.A: An S3 Object Lambda access point runs a Lambda function that redacts PII as the object is read, so the provider always sees the latest conversation with the PII removed, and it scales automatically with no copies.
x.B: A batch process on EC2 that regularly redacts files isn't up to the most recent conversation, and means managing a server and duplicate data.
x.C: A web application on EC2 means managing a server and building the application, and it scales poorly.
x.D: Storing non-PII data in DynamoDB through Lambda needs custom processing and a second data store, and doesn't hand over the conversations in the original form.

x.A: Termination protection stops accidental termination but doesn't help recover from a failure of the underlying hardware.
x.B: EC2 instances can't be configured for Multi-AZ, because an instance runs in one AZ.
x.C: A CloudWatch alarm with the EC2 recover action restarts the instance on healthy hardware when a system status check fails, keeping the same instance ID, IP addresses, and data. It improves recovery time without code changes or more instances.
x.D: RAID on EBS provides storage redundancy and doesn't help when the instance fails.

x.A: ECS with Service Auto Scaling, a minimum of 3, and a spread placement across AZs keeps tasks running in all three AZs, and it needs few changes to run the containers and little operational work.
x.B: EKS with self-managed nodes means managing the nodes and Kubernetes, which is more overhead.
x.C: EC2 instances in a spread placement group with an Auto Scaling group means managing instances and the container runtime, and a spread placement group isn't about AZs.
x.D: Lambda would need the application to be rewritten as functions, which is more than minimal changes.

x.A: Lifecycle policies move objects after set times, but they can't follow demand per movie, and Infrequent Access isn't the lowest cost for rarely watched movies.
x.B: Standard-IA is cheaper than Standard but costs more than Glacier for older movies, and standard retrieval isn't needed since IA is instant.
x.C: Intelligent-Tiering fits newer movies with changing demand, and older movies in Glacier Flexible Retrieval cost less. Expedited retrieval makes a movie available within 1 to 5 minutes, which meets the 5 minute requirement.
x.D: Bulk retrieval takes up to 5 to 12 hours, which doesn't meet the 5 minute requirement.

x.A: Lambda can't mount S3 as a volume, and Lambda's ephemeral storage is limited to 10 GB.
x.B: Lambda can't use EBS volumes, and 50 GB exceeds Lambda's temporary storage.
x.C: ECS on Fargate is serverless, runs the container image, and an EFS volume provides more than 50 GB of storage for temporary files, with no infrastructure to manage.
x.D: The EC2 launch type means managing EC2 instances, so it isn't serverless.

x.A: IAM Identity Center needs a SAML-compatible or supported directory and can't integrate with an LDAP that isn't SAML-compatible.
x.B: An IAM policy can't be integrated into LDAP to authenticate users.
x.C: Rotating IAM credentials when LDAP changes means long-term IAM credentials and manual syncing, which is insecure.
x.D: A custom identity broker authenticates users against LDAP and calls STS to get temporary credentials, which can be used to sign in to the console. It's the standard way to federate a non-SAML directory.

x.A: EBS snapshots of AMIs stored in another account need effort to create and manage, and recovering requires rebuilding the AMI.
x.B: Copying AMIs periodically is a manual process that needs to be kept up to date and costs more.
x.C: A Recycle Bin retention rule keeps deleted AMIs for a set time, so accidentally deleted ones can be recovered quickly with little setup.
x.D: AMIs can't simply be uploaded to S3 and replicated this way, and it takes more effort.

x.A: Snowmobile is for exabyte-scale data and is far too large and costly for 150 TB.
x.B: Several Snowball devices can carry 150 TB offline, which easily meets the 1 month deadline at a reasonable cost.
x.C: At 100 Mbps for part of each day, 150 TB would take well over a year, so Transfer Acceleration can't meet the deadline.
x.D: A VPN and a VPC endpoint are limited by the same 100 Mbps link.

x.A: Web and application tier VMs move to EC2 in private subnets, and the database moves to RDS for MySQL, which supports point-in-time restore. It's the fewest changes and least operational overhead.
x.B: Aurora MySQL changes the database engine and public subnets for the web tier isn't what the question asks. It's more change.
x.C: The web tier in a public subnet is reasonable, but the question mentions fewest changes, and the intended design keeps both tiers private behind a managed entry point.
x.D: Putting the database in public subnets isn't secure, and Aurora changes the engine.

x.A: An instance profile gives EC2 instances in the account permissions and doesn't give another company access to a queue.
x.B: An IAM policy in the development team's account applies to its own identities. The other company has its own account, so an identity-based policy wouldn't apply, and the company doesn't want to give up its own permissions.
x.C: An SQS access policy (resource-based policy) can grant another AWS account permission to poll the queue directly, without that company changing its own permissions.
x.D: An SNS access policy controls an SNS topic, not an SQS queue.

x.A: A bastion host in the private subnet isn't reachable from outside, and ec2:CreateVpnConnection isn't the permission for connecting to instances.
x.B: Site-to-Site VPNs plus extra VPNs for remote workers is complex and costly.
x.C: A bastion host in a public subnet needs SSH keys, security group management, and a running instance, which costs more and adds a larger attack surface.
x.D: Systems Manager Session Manager gives SSH-like access through IAM permissions, with no open ports, keys, or bastion hosts. It needs the SSM agent (on Amazon Linux) and the managed instance policy, and it costs nothing extra.

x.A: DataSync with a cron job copies data to S3 but doesn't give researchers immediate local access to the frequently used subset.
x.B: A file gateway presents NFS or SMB files, but the researchers' data are on storage arrays as block volumes, and a file gateway isn't designed for that.
x.C: A volume gateway with cached volumes stores the full dataset in S3 and caches the frequently accessed subset locally, so researchers get immediate access, and capital expenses fall since most data is in AWS.
x.D: A VPN to EFS has higher latency for the subset and doesn't give local caching.

x.A: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery lets you restore to any second in the last 35 days, so reverting within 24 hours is covered by turning on one setting.
x.B: AWS Backup works, but it takes snapshot-based backups on a schedule, so it can't revert to any point in time within the last 24 hours.
x.C: Hourly on-demand backups with Lambda can't restore to any point in time and need code to maintain.
x.D: Streams capture changes but don't restore a table, and managing the log means more work.

x.A: CloudTrail and AppSync aren't built to process uploaded files, and it adds complexity.
x.B: An S3 object-created event invokes a Lambda function for each upload. Lambda scales from a few files an hour to hundreds of concurrent uploads, and the 5 second processing is cheap, since you pay per run.
x.C: Kinesis Data Streams isn't needed for files and costs while running, even when there are few uploads.
x.D: SNS doesn't process the files, and adding it to the path only adds a service.

x.A: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option and aren't aimed at saving cost.
x.B: Reserved Instances for nonproduction waste money because the instances are shut down part of the time, so the reservation isn't fully used.
x.C: Compute Savings Plans discount the constant production usage (including Lambda), and On-Demand Instances that are shut down when not used avoid paying for idle nonproduction time.
x.D: Dedicated Hosts for production are costly, and an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for nonproduction instances that run only part of the time isn't a good fit.

x.A: A full-load task migrates the data once and doesn't capture changes that occur during the migration.
x.B: DataSync copies files and isn't used to migrate a relational database with change capture.
x.C: SCT converts the Oracle schema to PostgreSQL, and DMS migrates the existing data and replicates ongoing changes (CDC), so changes during migration are captured.
x.D: Snowball and the aws_s3 import is a one-time load without ongoing change capture.

x.A: ECS with Fargate runs containers with no servers to manage, and services scale in and out with demand.
x.B: EKS with Fargate also runs pods without managing nodes, and scales with demand.
x.C: API Gateway and Lambda don't run containers in the way described, and it isn't a container hosting solution.
x.D: ECS with EC2 worker nodes means managing the EC2 instances, which adds operational overhead.
x.E: EKS with EC2 worker nodes means managing nodes and clusters, which adds overhead.

x.A: A large group with half the instances stopped would still pay for the EBS storage, and Auto Scaling can't use stopped instances to scale out that way.
x.B: Setting the minimum size to peak levels means paying for peak capacity the whole time, which is expensive.
x.C: Caching dynamic content and scaling in after populating is unreliable, because the cache wouldn't hold during the sale, and it isn't cost-effective.
x.D: An Auto Scaling group that scales out as traffic increases, using a launch template with a preconfigured AMI, adds instances quickly only when needed, which is the most cost-effective.

x.A: A custom Lambda script has to be written, run, and maintained, which is more overhead.
x.B: The AWS Config managed rule restricted-ssh checks whether security groups allow unrestricted SSH, and it can notify through SNS when a noncompliant rule is created. It can be enabled right away with no code.
x.C: An IAM role with permissions to open security groups doesn't detect or prevent a breach, and notifying on assuming the role is not the requirement.
x.D: An SCP that blocks all non-admin users from editing security groups is heavy-handed and doesn't detect an open SSH rule.

x.A: An inspection VPC with Network Firewall and a transit gateway enforces HTTPS but doesn't provide a service registry for discovery, and it takes a lot of setup.
x.B: VPC Lattice provides service-to-service communication across VPCs and accounts for Lambda and EKS services, with HTTPS listeners and a built-in service registry for discovery, with little administration.
x.C: An NLB and PrivateLink for each microservice means a lot of resources to create and manage, and it doesn't provide service discovery.
x.D: Peering connections between many VPCs, prefix lists, and route tables is complex and doesn't offer a service registry.
